introduction-the-unpatchable-vulnerabili.core: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than software: authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness, curiosity and reciprocity. People can't be patched, and most breaches involve a human element (Verizon DBIR). Defence therefore combines technology that removes the human single point of failure (phishing-resistant MFA, least privilege, verification workflows) with a culture where reporting and challenging is easy and blame-free.

first_principles.problem: A firm with strong firewalls is breached when a help-desk agent resets an executive's MFA for a convincing caller.
derivation: Remove **single human approvals** for risky actions.

analogy.title: A con artist at the castle gate
analogy.story: The walls are thick, but a confident stranger in a messenger's uniform talks the guard into opening up.
analogy.breaks: Guards can be retrained quickly; organisations have thousands of 'guards' with varied awareness.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A convincing voice alone can't reset MFA.

code.text:
MFA reset requests:
1. Never act on inbound calls alone
2. Call back on the number in the HR directory
3. Require manager approval in the ticket
4. Executives: in-person or video with ID check
5. Log and alert security on every reset

check.q: Why is phishing-resistant MFA a social engineering defence?
check.a: Even if a user is tricked into entering credentials, FIDO2 won't authenticate to the attacker's fake domain.

phishing-the-digital-lure.core: Phishing uses deceptive messages to make people click links, open attachments or enter credentials. Mass phishing casts wide; spear phishing targets individuals with researched details; whaling targets executives; business email compromise (BEC) impersonates partners to redirect payments. Modern kits proxy real login pages (adversary-in-the-middle) to steal session cookies and bypass OTP MFA. Defences include SPF/DKIM/DMARC, link and attachment sandboxing, FIDO2 MFA, external-sender banners and one-click reporting.

first_principles.problem: Finance pays a fake 'updated bank details' invoice from a lookalike supplier domain, losing $400k.
truths: Email sender identity is easy to fake.

analogy.title: A fishing lure that looks like real food
analogy.story: The fish sees a tasty insect; only on biting does it find the hook.
analogy.breaks: Fish can't call the insect back to check; people can verify through another channel.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Spoofed mail claiming your exact domain is rejected.

code.text:
_dmarc.example.com. TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; adkim=s; aspf=s"
example.com.        TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all"

points: Verify payment changes out of band.

check.q: Does DMARC stop lookalike domains like examp1e.com?
check.a: No. It protects your exact domain; lookalikes need monitoring, banners and user verification.

vishing-and-smishing-voice-and-sms-attac.core: Vishing (voice phishing) and smishing (SMS phishing) move the lure to phones, where caller ID and sender names are easily spoofed and people react faster. Attackers pose as IT support, banks or executives, sometimes with AI voice cloning, to get MFA codes, password resets or remote-access installs. SIM-swap attacks hijack phone numbers to intercept SMS codes. Defences are callback verification, never sharing codes, phishing-resistant MFA instead of SMS, and carrier SIM locks.

first_principles.problem: An employee gets a text 'IT: approve the MFA prompt to keep your account', then a call from 'support', and approves the attacker's login.
truths: SMS codes can be intercepted or relayed.
derivation: **Hang up and call back** on known numbers.
Publish how **IT will actually** contact staff.

analogy.title: A phone call from 'your bank' asking you to read your PIN
analogy.story: The bank already knows what it needs; a real one never asks you to read secrets aloud.
mapping: Calling the number on your card
analogy.breaks: Voice cloning now makes even familiar voices untrustworthy.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Staff have a clear rule to fall back on under pressure.

code.text:
IT will NEVER:
- ask for your password or MFA code
- ask you to approve a prompt you didn't start
- text you a link to 'verify' your account
If unsure: hang up, call the service desk on x4000

check.q: Why is SMS a weak MFA factor?
check.a: SIM swaps, SS7 interception and social engineering can redirect or obtain the codes.

pretexting-the-long-con.core: Pretexting is building a believable fabricated scenario (the pretext) to win trust and extract information or access, often over multiple interactions. The attacker researches the target via LinkedIn, org charts and press releases, then plays a role such as auditor, new hire, vendor or recruiter. Each small request seems harmless, but together they build access. Defences are identity verification procedures, need-to-know information policies, and a culture where checking is polite, not rude.

first_principles.problem: A 'new contractor' builds rapport with an engineer over two weeks, then asks them to 'just add me to the repo while my access is stuck'.

analogy.title: An actor fully in character
analogy.story: They don't just wear a costume; they know the jargon, names and backstory well enough that nobody questions them.
analogy.breaks: Theatre audiences know it's fiction; targets don't.

example.title: Access request rule

code.text:
Repo/system access is ONLY granted when:
- a ticket exists from the requester's manager
- identity is confirmed in the HR system
- no one grants access as a personal favour

example.outcome: long cons fail at the gate.

check.q: Why do pretexters make small requests first?
check.a: Each compliance builds commitment and trust, making the larger request feel normal (foot-in-the-door).

baiting-and-quid-pro-quo-exploiting-gree.core: Baiting offers something enticing, such as a USB stick labelled 'Salaries 2025' left in the car park, a free download or a gift card, so that curiosity or greed leads the victim to run malware or give data. Quid pro quo offers a service in exchange: 'free IT help' in return for disabling antivirus or sharing a login. Both exploit reciprocity and curiosity. Defences include blocking USB mass storage and auto-run, application allow-listing, and teaching that unexpected gifts and help are red flags.

first_principles.problem: An employee plugs in a found USB drive marked 'Confidential – Layoffs', which emulates a keyboard and installs a backdoor.
derivation: Block **USB storage** and HID-injection via device control.
Only accept IT help via **official tickets**.

analogy.title: The Trojan horse
analogy.story: A gift too good to refuse is wheeled inside the gates, carrying soldiers.
analogy.breaks: Troy took one horse; USB drops cost pennies and can be scattered widely.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Unknown USB devices are blocked even if plugged in.

code.text:
# USBGuard: block new USB devices by default
usbguard generate-policy > /etc/usbguard/rules.conf   # allow current ones
systemctl enable --now usbguard
# Windows GPO: Removable Storage Access → Deny all

check.q: Why doesn't disabling auto-run stop a 'Rubber Ducky' USB?
check.a: It presents as a keyboard and types commands, which device control or HID policies must block.

physical-security-tailgating-and-piggyba.core: Physical social engineering gets attackers into buildings: tailgating (following someone through a door unnoticed) and piggybacking (being let in, perhaps carrying boxes or posing as a courier). Inside, they can plant devices, photograph screens, steal laptops or plug into network ports. Defences include mantraps and turnstiles, visible badges, visitor escorts, locked server rooms, clean-desk and screen-lock policies, 802.1X on network ports, and staff who feel empowered to ask 'can I see your badge?'.

first_principles.problem: A 'delivery driver' with a box is held the door, then plugs a rogue device into a meeting-room network port.
truths: Network ports trust whatever plugs in.

analogy.title: Holding the door for the person behind you
analogy.story: It's a kind habit, and that kindness is exactly what the attacker counts on.
analogy.breaks: Courtesy is good in daily life; in secure areas it must be overridden by policy.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A rogue device gets no network even if plugged in.

code.text:
interface Gi1/0/12
  authentication port-control auto
  dot1x pae authenticator
  ! unknown devices land in a quarantine VLAN with no access

check.q: What's the difference between tailgating and piggybacking?
check.a: Tailgating is following without the employee's knowledge; piggybacking is with their consent, usually via a pretext.

building-organizational-defenses-against.core: Durable defence against social engineering is a system, not an annual video. Remove human single points of failure with technical controls (FIDO2 MFA, least privilege, payment dual-approval), define verification procedures for risky requests, run frequent realistic simulations, and measure reporting rate more than click rate. Crucially, build a no-blame culture: people who report a mistake fast limit damage, and punishing clicks only teaches hiding.

first_principles.problem: Annual compliance training is completed by 100% of staff, yet phishing click rates don't improve and nobody reports incidents.

analogy.title: Aviation's safety culture
analogy.story: Pilots report near-misses without punishment, so the whole industry learns and improves.
analogy.breaks: Aviation has regulators enforcing it; companies must choose to build this culture.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Focus shifts to fast detection by people.

code.text:
| Metric                  | Q1   | Q4 target |
|-------------------------|------|-----------|
| Simulation click rate   | 14%  | < 5%      |
| Report rate             | 9%   | > 60%     |
| Median time to report   | 3 h  | < 10 min  |
| Accounts with FIDO2     | 20%  | 100% admin|

check.q: Why measure report rate over click rate?
check.a: Fast reports let security contain an attack even after someone clicks; it measures the human detection layer.
